newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak FinMin says mulling import surcharge - paper.
newsitem.headline: Slovak FinMin says mulling import surcharge - paper.

text.p: Slovakia is considering introducing an import surcharge to replace the current import deposit scheme, Finance Minister Sergej Kozlik told daily Slovenska Republika on Tuesday.
"There are signs that some international institutions would accept import surcharge...We will negotiate this further on," Kozlik said.
The government imposed the import deposit plan for selected goods in May, saying it was a direct reaction to similar plans approved earlier by the Czech government.

According to the scheme, all importers of certain specified goods must place a sum equal to 20 percent of the value of the imports in interest-free accounts in the central bank through the state-run Konsolidacna Banka s.p.u., for 180 days.
Kozlik said Slovakia would not stick to this measure, but must, however, deal with negative trade balance.
"We imposed deposits in order to balance our trade relations with the Czech Republic within the framework of the customs union," he said.
The Czech Republic is Slovakia's largest trading partner, accounting for around 30 percent of overall Slovak exports.
"If the Czech Republic abolishes its measures, we are ready to abolish ours, in two weeks," Kozlik said.
Czech officials have said they may cancel the plan as of October.
The Slovak trade deficit totalled 27.908 billion crowns ($836 million) for the January-April period, up from 21.498 billion for the same period in 1996.
"On the other hand, we are notifying the European Union that there are problems with the trade balance and therefore we must seek for certain measures," he added.

In June, the government announced that it was planning a series of measures to help the economy, including wage regulations, tax breaks for foreign investors and an increase in taxes on hydrocarbon fuels.
Kozlik said the package would include also the government's proposal of the law on protection against excessive imports and the law on protection against subsidised imports.
